name: discrete-probability
summary: Exact discrete-probability calculations (birthday-paradox collisions, dice-sum distributions, drawing without replacement, binomial trials, Bayes' theorem, generalized Monty Hall) plus statistically rigorous two-proportion comparison (a z-test, Wilson/Newcombe confidence intervals, and a plain verdict), exposed as an MCP server, each answer optionally cross-checked against a real CSPRNG-backed simulation.
problem: Language models are well-documented to be unreliable at discrete probability, and specifically worse on 'counterintuitive' problems: a 2026 study on counterintuitive discrete-probability problems found models average 0.96 accuracy on standard problems but only 0.59 on counterintuitive ones (arxiv.org/pdf/2606.07516), and the widely-discussed 'LLMs Can't Do Probability' writeup documents the same failure informally. The birthday paradox and the Monty Hall problem are the canonical examples of a single correct answer that both humans and models reliably get wrong by reasoning about it instead of calculating it. Separately, comparing two observed rates (e.g. two win rates over N trials) by eye, without a real significance test, routinely mistakes noise for a real effect or vice versa -- the owner's own AI-TCG balance-testing workflow hand-rolls exactly this comparison every cycle (special-projects/wishlist.md, 2026-09-24).
